claim: OGT is an essential enzyme that mediates protein O-GlcNAcylation, a unique form of posttranslational modification of many nuclear and cytosolic proteins.
source: The O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) is an essential enzyme that mediates protein O-GlcNAcylation, a unique form of posttranslational modification of many nuclear and cytosolic proteins.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, representing consensus understanding of OGT function.

claim: Recent studies observed increased OGT and O-GlcNAcylation levels in a broad range of human cancer tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues.
source: Recent studies observed increased OGT and O-GlcNAcylation levels in a broad range of human cancer tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues, indicating a universal effect of OGT in promoting tumorigenesis.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings without specific citations in this sentence, representing established observations in the field.

claim: Deletion of OGT caused a marked reduction in tumor growth in both syngeneic mice tumor models and a genetic mice colorectal cancer model induced by mutation of the Apc gene.
source: We found that deletion of OGT (Ogt−/−) caused a marked reduction in tumor growth in both syngeneic mice tumor models and a genetic mice colorectal cancer (CRC) model induced by mutation of the Apc gene (Apcmin).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse models described in the manuscript.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of OGT induced robust genomic instability leading to cGAS-dependent production of type I interferon and IFN-stimulated genes.
source: Pharmacological inhibition or genetic deletion of OGT induced a robust genomic instability (GIN), leading to cGAS-dependent production of the type I interferon (IFN-I) and IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the effects of OGT inhibition/deletion on genomic stability and immune signaling.

claim: Deletion of Cgas or Sting from Ogt−/− cancer cells restored tumor growth and correlated with impaired CD8+ T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity.
source: As a result, deletion of Cgas or Sting from Ogt−/− cancer cells restored tumor growth, and this correlated with impaired CD8+ T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from double knockout experiments showing rescue of tumor growth.

claim: OGT-dependent cleavage of host cell factor C1 (HCF-1) is required for the avoidance of genomic instability and IFN-I production in tumors.
source: Mechanistically, we found that OGT-dependent cleavage of host cell factor C1 (HCF-1) is required for the avoidance of GIN and IFN-I production in tumors.
evidence: This mechanistic claim is supported by experimental data showing the role of HCF-1 cleavage in the OGT pathway.

claim: Protein modification by O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine is a dynamic and reversible post-translational modification added by O-GlcNAc transferase and removed by O-GlcNAcase.
source: Protein modification by the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) is a dynamic and reversible post-translational modification, which is added to the hydroxyl group of a specific serine or threonine residue in a target protein by O-GlcNAc transferase (OGT) and removed by O-GlcNAcase (OGA; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2018 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation modifies thousands of cytoplasmic, nuclear, and mitochondrial proteins and mediates crosstalk with protein phosphorylation.
source: O-GlcNAcylation is a fast-cycle and nutrient-sensitive PTM, which modifies thousands of cytoplasmic, nuclear, and mitochondrial proteins and mediates crosstalk with protein phosphorylation, regulating signal transduction and affecting protein localization, activity, stability, and protein-protein interaction.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about O-GlcNAcylation function based on prior research.

claim: Dysregulation of O-GlcNAcylation is associated with multiple metabolic diseases and cancer.
source: Dysregulation of O-GlcNAcylation is associated with multiple metabolic diseases and cancer (Li et al., 2019; Zhu and Hart, 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2019 and Zhu and Hart, 2023.

claim: Increased OGT and O-GlcNAcylation levels were observed in human colon cancer tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues.
source: Recent studies observed increased OGT and O-GlcNAcylation level in human colon cancer tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues (Mi et al., 2011; Phueaouan et al., 2013; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2014), indicating an essential role of OGT-mediated protein O-GlcNAcylation in the pathogenesis of colon cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mi et al., 2011; Phueaouan et al., 2013; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2014.

claim: Several oncogenic proteins involved in colon cancer pathogenesis, including β-catenin and NF-κB, are directly modified by O-GlcNAc.
source: Several oncogenic proteins that are involved in the pathogenesis of colon cancer have been shown to be directly modified by O-GlcNAc, including β-catenin and NF-κB (Fardini et al., 2013; Chaiyawat et al., 2014; Ozcan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fardini et al., 2013; Chaiyawat et al., 2014; Ozcan et al., 2010.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation of β-catenin at T41 inhibits its phosphorylation, which attenuates its ubiquitination and degradation and promotes oncogenic activity.
source: For example, O-GlcNAcylation of β-catenin at T41 inhibits its phosphorylation, which subsequently attenuates its ubiquitination and degradation and promotes oncogenic activity (Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2014; Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Olivier-Van Stichelen et al., 2014 and 2012.

claim: Inhibitory roles of O-GlcNAc signaling in the growth of human colon cancer and in oncogenic Wnt/β-catenin signaling have been reported.
source: In contrast, inhibitory roles of O-GlcNAc signaling in the growth of human colon cancer and in oncogenic Wnt/β-catenin signaling have also been reported (Yehezkel et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yehezkel et al., 2012 and Wu et al., 2014.

claim: The cGAS/STING cytosolic DNA-sensing pathway plays a vital role in activating the innate immune response and production of type I interferons.
source: The cGAS/STING cytosolic DNA-sensing pathway plays a vital role in activating the innate immune response and production of the type I interferons (IFN-I) (Li et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2023 and represents established knowledge.

claim: cGAS interacts with cytosolic double-stranded DNA in a sequence-independent manner.
source: Cyclic guanosine monophosphate (GMP)–adenosine monophosphate (AMP) synthase (cGAS) interacts with cytosolic double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) in a sequence-independent manner.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about cGAS function.

claim: Direct binding of cGAS to cytosolic dsDNA promotes cGAS homodimerization and activates the catalytic activity of cGAS, producing 2', 3'-cyclic GMP-AMP from ATP and GTP.
source: The direct binding of cGAS to cytosolic dsDNA promotes cGAS homodimerization and activates the catalytic activity of cGAS, producing 2', 3'-cyclic GMP-AMP (cGAMP) from ATP and GTP.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the cGAS mechanism.

claim: The second messenger cGAMP binds to and activates STING, which then translocates to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment to recruit TBK1 and IRF3, leading to IFN-I production and activation of ISGs.
source: The second messenger cGAMP binds to and activates the endoplasmic resident stimulator of interferon genes (STING). Once activated, STING translocates to the ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) to recruit TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) and IFN regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), leading to the production of IFN-I and activation of numerous IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs; Ghosh et al., 2021; Fang et al., 2023; Kwon and Bakhoum, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ghosh et al., 2021; Fang et al., 2023; Kwon and Bakhoum, 2020 and represents established knowledge.

claim: OGT mRNA expression shows a significant positive correlation with tumorigenesis in multiple cancer types including BLCA, CHOL, COAD, ESCA, HNSC, LIHC, LUAD, PRAD, READ, SARC, and STAD.
source: Initial analysis of data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) dataset in GEPIA2 (http://gepia2.cancer-pku.cn/#index) and found a significant positive correlation between OGT mRNA expression and tumorigenesis in bladder urothelial carcinoma (BLCA), cholangiocarcinoma (CHOL), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), esophageal carcinoma (ESCA), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), kidney chromophobe (LIHC), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD), rectum adenocarcinoma (READ), sarcoma (SARC), and a stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: OGT mRNA expression was significantly increased in COAD samples compared to adjacent or normal samples.
source: Next, we utilized UALCAN database analysis, and found that OGT mRNA expression was compared between 286 COAD samples and 41 adjacent or normal samples, the expression of OGT was significantly increased in COAD at the transcriptional level (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by UALCAN database analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Stage IV COAD tissues exhibited the highest expression level of OGT compared with lower stages.
source: A significant positive correlation tendency between OGT mRNA expression and individual different tumor stages was observed. The stage IV COAD tissues exhibited the highest expression level of OGT in compared with low stage (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: A significant positive correlation exists between OGT mRNA expression and nodal metastasis status.
source: We also observed a significant positive correlation between OGT mRNA expression and nodal metastasis status (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The protein level of OGT was significantly increased in COAD patient samples and amongst individual different stages based on CPTAC and HPA online databases.
source: Furthermore, we found that the protein level of OGT was also significantly increased in COAD patient samples and amongst individual different stages based on the CPTAC and HPA online database (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from CPTAC and HPA databases shown in Figure 1D–F.

claim: Intestinal OGT protein was markedly increased in Apcmin mouse tumor tissues compared to adjacent or normal tissues.
source: Intestinal OGT protein was markedly increased in Apcmin mouse tumor tissues compared to adjacent or normal tissues (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: O-GlcNAcylation protein levels in intestinal tissues were significantly higher in tumor tissues than adjacent or normal tissues in Apcmin mice.
source: As expected, O-GlcNAcylation proteins levels in intestinal tissues were also significantly higher in tumor tissues than adjacent or normal tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data from Apcmin mouse tissues.

claim: Mouse OGT protein was markedly higher in tumor tissues than in adjacent tissues as shown by IHC staining.
source: IHC staining revealed that mouse OGT protein was markedly higher in tumor tissues than in adjacent tissues (Figure 1H), which was consistent with the expression pattern in human samples.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: OGT protein was upregulated in the azoxymethane (AOM)/dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) colorectal tumor model.
source: OGT protein was also upregulated in the azoxymethane (AOM)/dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) colorectal tumor model (Figure 1I–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I–K.

claim: Intestinal OGT levels were drastically decreased in Ogt IEC cKO Apcmin mice compared to wildtype Apcmin mice.
source: Intestinal OGT levels were drastically decreased in Ogt IEC cKO Apcmin mice compared to wildtype Apcmin mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Deletion of Ogt in intestinal epithelial cells resulted in significantly reduced tumor size and total number of polyps at 20 weeks of age.
source: Importantly, deletion of the Ogt in intestinal epithelial cells resulted in significantly reduced tumor size and total number of polyps at 20 weeks of age (Figure 2A), indicating that OGT promotes oncogenic transformation in colorectal tumor in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor measurement data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Epithelial inflammation increased in Ogt IEC cKO Apcmin mice compared to wildtype Apcmin mice as demonstrated by H&E staining.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining demonstrated that epithelial inflammation increased in Ogt IEC cKO Apcmin mice compared to wildtype Apcmin mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: OGT deficiency in intestinal tissues was associated with significantly elevated gene expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines Il1a, Il6, TNFa, and interferons/ISGs like Isg15, Mx1, Cxcl10.
source: OGT deficiency in intestinal tissues was also associated with significantly elevated gene expression of key pro-inflammatory cytokines like interleukin Il1a, Il6, TNFa, as well as several interferons and ISGs like Isg15, Mx1, Cxcl10 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: IL-2, IL-6, IL-10, IL-17, IFN-α, IFN-β, IFN-γ, and CXCL10 were upregulated in Ogt IEC cKO Apcmin mice compared with control mice.
source: Furthermore, we found IL-2, IL-6, IL-10, IL-17, IFN-α, IFN-β, IFN-γ, and CXCL10 were upregulated compared with control mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Isg15, Mx1, and Ifnb1 mRNA expression were significantly increased in all cultured Ogt knockout cells (MC38, LLC, B16-OVA, HT29) except Ifna4.
source: We then evaluated the expression changes of Ifna4, Ifnb1, Isg15, Mx1 and found that all the genes except Ifna4 mRNA expression were significantly increased in all cultured Ogt knockout cells (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: Phosphorylation of STAT1, TBK1 and IRF3 is increased while STING expression is reduced in Ogt knockout MC38, LLC, B16-OVA, and HT29 cells.
source: We found that while the phosphorylation of STAT1, TBK1 and IRF3 is increased, the STING expression is reduced in Ogt knockout MC38, LLC, B16-OVA, and HT29 cells (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E–F.

claim: Expression of exogenous OGT in Ogt knockout cells abolished the type I IFN pathway activation effect.
source: To determine whether this effect is specific for Ogt knockout, we stably expressed exogenous OGT in Ogt knockout cells and found that the type I IFN pathway activation effect is abolished (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Knockout of MAVS in Ogt−/− cells has no effect on Isg15, Mx1, Ifna4 and Ifnb1 expression or the type I IFN pathway.
source: In order to eliminate the type I IFN pathway activate independent on RNA but dependent on dsDNA, we knocked out MAVS protein in Ogt−/− cells, which is a RNA pivotal adaptor protein activate the downstream protein kinase TBK1, IFN pathway and ISGs in Ogt−/− cells (24), and we found that knockout of MAVS in Ogt−/− cells has no effect on either Isg15, Mx1, Ifna4 and Ifnb1 expression or the type I IFN pathway (Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from MAVS knockout experiments shown in Figure 3G–H.

claim: Type I IFN and Cxcl10 signals disappeared in OGT/cGAS and OGT/STING double knockout cells at both mRNA and protein levels.
source: Surprisingly, these type I IFN and Cxcl10 signals disappeared in OGT/cGAS and OGT/STING double knockout cells both in mRNA and protein level (Figure 3I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR, ELISA, and western blot data shown in Figure 3I–L.

claim: BMDCs pre-cultured with Ogt+/+ or Ogt−/− B16-OVA tumor cell supernatant provided a potent activated signal for optimal single epitope-specific T cell proliferation.
source: The results showed that BMDCs pre-cultured with Ogt+/+ or Ogt−/− B16-OVA tumor cells supernatant provided a potent activated signal for optimal single epitope-specific T cell proliferation (Figure 3M), while cGAS or STING deficiency in Ogt−/− tumor cells diminished such effects (Figure 3N).
evidence: This claim is supported by T cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: cGAS or STING deficiency in Ogt−/− tumor cells diminished the activated signal for T cell proliferation.
source: The results showed that BMDCs pre-cultured with Ogt+/+ or Ogt−/− B16-OVA tumor cells supernatant provided a potent activated signal for optimal single epitope-specific T cell proliferation (Figure 3M), while cGAS or STING deficiency in Ogt−/− tumor cells diminished such effects (Figure 3N).
evidence: This claim is supported by T cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3N.

claim: Cell proliferation was abolished when Ifnar1-/- BMDCs were pre-cultured with Ogt+/+ or Ogt−/− B16-OVA tumor cell supernatant.
source: Further, we added the supernatant from Ogt+/+ or Ogt−/− B16-OVA tumor cells into the co-culture system of Ifnar1 knockout BMDCs and OT-I cells. The cell proliferation was abolished when treated with Ifnar1-/- BMDCs pre-cultured with Ogt+/+ or Ogt−/− B16-OVA tumor cells supernatant. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by T cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: γH2AX was dramatically increased in Ogt knockout MC38, LLC, HT29 and B16-OVA cells.
source: We next assessed the phosphorylation of H2AX at Ser 139 (γH2AX), an indirect marker of DNA DSBs in the cell lines (Chowdhury et al., 2005). Comparable expression levels of H2AX, we found that γH2AX was dramatically increased in Ogt knockout MC38, LLC, HT29 and B16-OVA cells (Figure 4C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C and F.

claim: Ogt knockout significantly induced immense DNA strand breakage in MC38 cells as shown by anti-γH2AX immunofluorescence staining and comet assays.
source: We also used the anti-γH2AX immunofluorescence staining and comet assays, a classical quantifying and analyzing DNA damage, and found that Ogt knockout significantly induced immense DNA strand breakage in MC38 cells (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and comet assay data shown in Figure 4D–E.

claim: Exogenous OGT expression abolished γH2AX expression in MC38, LLC, HT29 and B16-OVA cells and DNA damage in MC38 cells.
source: Finally, the rescued results showed that exogenous OGT expression abolished the γH2AX expression both in MC38, LLC, HT29 and B16-OVA cells and DNA damage in MC38 cells (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 4F–H.

claim: HCF-1 was the most enriched protein in the precipitates from OGT restored HT29 knockout cells compared to OGT knockout cells reconstituted with empty vector.
source: Next, we use GFP agarose immunoprecipitation and liquid chromatography coupled to tandem MS (LC-MS/MS) to identify different proteins that interacted with OGT in human colonic cancer cell line HT29. Interestingly, HCF-1 was the most enriched protein in the precipitates from OGT restored HT29 knockout cells compared to OGT knockout cells reconstituted with empty vector, based on the number of peptides (indicating the identification confidence) and the number of peptide-spectrum matches (PSMs, indicating the abundance; Figure 5A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Human HCF-1 undergoes proteolytic maturation by OGT cleavage resulting in stably associated HCF-1N1011 and HCF-1C600 subunits that regulate different aspects of the cell cycle.
source: Previous studies showed that the human epigenetic cell-cycle regulator (HCF-1) undergoes an unusual proteolytic maturation by OGT cleavage and process resulting in stably associated HCF-1N1011 and HCF-1C600 subunits that regulate different aspects of the cell cycle (Capotosti et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Capotosti et al., 2011.

claim: OGT can bind HCF-1C600.
source: To clarify how to OGT regulate function of HCF-1, we transfected empty vector (EV), the full-length HCF-1-HA (HCF-1FL), HCF-11-1011-HA (HCF-1N1011), HCF-11-450-HA (HCF-1N450), HCF-1450-1011-HA (HCF-1N450-1011) and HCF-11436-2035-HA (HCF-1C600) and myc-OGT and found that OGT can bind HCF-1C600 (Figure 5E), furthermore OGT directly bind the HCF-1C600 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5E and pull-down assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: HCF-1C600 can restore gene expression differences of Isg15, Mx1 and Ifnb1 in OGT knockout cells, while HCF-1FL and HCF-1N1011 cannot.
source: To further understand the physiological function of HCF-1, we transfected EV, HCF-1FL, HCF-1N1011and HCF-1C600 into MC38 control and OGT knockout cells, respectively. As shown in Figure 5F, transfected HCF-1FL and HCF-1N1011 didn't rescue the gene expression differences, such as Isg15, Mx1 and Ifnb1, but HCF-1C600 can restore the gene expression differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: HCF-1C600 can eliminate cytosolic DNA accumulation, DNA damage, and type I IFN activation in Ogt knockout cells.
source: These results were confirmed by using western blot and anti-dsDNA immunofluorescence staining (Figure 5G–H). Overall, these data indicated that OGT regulates the HCF-1 cleavage and maturation, HCF-1C600 can eliminate the cytosolic DNA accumulation, DNA damage, the type I IFN activation and restrain cGAS-STING-mediated DNA sensing.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5G–H.

claim: Ogt deficiency MC38 colorectal tumor cells have no obvious inhibition of cell growth in vitro.
source: We found that the Ogt deficiency MC38 colorectal tumor cells have no obvious inhibit cell growth in vitro (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro cell proliferation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ogt deficiency resulted in significant delay in tumor growth, reduced tumor weight and prolonged mice survival in MC38 tumor model.
source: However, we found that a significant delay in tumor growth, tumor weight and prolong mice survival compared to the control group (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: Ogt deficiency delayed tumor growth and prolonged survival in LLC and B16-OVA tumor models.
source: We also used lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) cells and the B16-OVA melanoma cells because they represent an aggressive murine tumor model and are highly resistant to various immunotherapies, similar results were shown in Figure 6C–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E. These results showed that Ogt deficiency could delay tumor growth and prolong survival of mice in MC38, LLC, and B16-OVA tumor model.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 6C–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: Tumors from C57BL/6 mice bearing Ogt−/− MC38 tumors showed higher proportion of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, functional CD8+ IFN-γ+, CD8+ TNF-α+ and CD8+ IFN-γ+ TNF-α+ double positive T cells compared to control tumors.
source: Consistently, tumors from C57BL/6 immunocompetent mice bearing Ogt−/− MC38 tumors compared with MC38 control tumors, showed higher proportion of CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, functional CD8+ IFN-γ+, CD8+ TNF-α+ and CD8+ IFN-γ+ TNF-α+ double positive T cells, but not CD45+, CD11b+ CD11c+, CD11b+ F4/80+, CD11b+ Ly6C+ and Treg cells (Figure 6E–H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E–H and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: The difference in tumor growth rate between MC38-Ogt knockout and control cells disappeared in immunodeficient Rag2–/– mice.
source: To determine whether Ogt deficiency is dependent upon adaptive immune system, we inoculated MC38 control and Ogt knockout cells into immunodeficient Rag2–/– mice and tracked tumor growth. The difference of tumor growth rate disappeared between MC38-Ogt knockout and control ones (Figure 6I), indicating their association with an impaired immune response.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth data in Rag2–/– mice shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Depletion of CD8+ T cells dramatically enhanced tumor growth in Ogt−/− tumor-bearing mice and eliminated the antitumor activity of Ogt deficiency.
source: Depletion CD8+ T cells dramatically enhanced the tumor growth in Ogt−/− tumor-bearing mice, compared to the isotype antibody treatment group, and their antitumor activity of Ogt deficiency disappeared, both in tumor volume, weight and survival curve (Figure 6J–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD8+ T cell depletion experiment data shown in Figure 6J–K.

claim: Depletion of CD4+ T cells had no obvious effect on tumor volume and weight in Ogt−/− tumor-bearing mice.
source: However, depletion CD4+ T cells have no obvious effect both in tumor volume and weight in Ogt−/− tumor-bearing mice, compared to the isotype antibody treatment group (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD4+ T cell depletion experiment data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Decreased tumor growth and prolonged mice survival phenotype disappeared in OGT rescued cells and in OGT/cGAS or OGT/STING double knockout tumors.
source: Next, to determine whether this effect is specific for OGT knockout, we performed this experiment in vivo using MC38 tumor-bearing rescue model. As we expected, decreased tumor growth and prolong mice survival phenotype disappeared both in OGT rescued cells (Figure 6L–M) and in OGT/cGAS or OGT/STING double knockout tumors (Figure 6N–O).
evidence: This claim is supported by rescue and double knockout experiment data shown in Figure 6L–O.

claim: The proportion of CD4+ T and CD8+ T cells, CD8+ IFN-γ+ and CD8+ TNF-α+ disappeared in OGT rescued cells and in OGT/cGAS or OGT/STING double knockout tumors in vivo.
source: Furthermore, flow cytometry results showed that the proportion of CD4+ T and CD8+ T cells, CD8+ IFN-γ+ and CD8+ TNF-α+ disappeared both in OGT rescued cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B-D) and in OGT/cGAS or OGT/STING double knockout tumors in vivo (Figure 6P and Figure 6—figure supplement 3E-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6P and Figure 6—figure supplement 3B-F.

claim: Deletion of Ogt synergized with PD-L1 blockade treatments to improve antitumor immunity in MC38 and LLC tumor models.
source: MC38 and LLC tumor growth was significantly delayed in tumor-bearing mice treated with PD-L1 antibody compared to isotype control (Figure 6Q and Figure 6—figure supplement 3G), which translated into extended survival (Figure 6R and Figure 6—figure supplement 3H). Deletion of Ogt synergized with PD-L1 blockade treatments to improve antitumor immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by combination therapy data shown in Figure 6Q, R and Figure 6—figure supplement 3G, H.

claim: Low OGT expression was associated with improved overall survival and progression free survival in patients with COAD.
source: We next assessed the potential relevance of OGT in human cancer immunity. We first analyzed gene expression profiles of cancer patients from TCGA database and survival, we found that low OGT expression was associated with improved overall survival (OS) and progression free survival (PFS) in patients with COAD (Figure 6S, T).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA survival analysis data shown in Figure 6S, T.

claim: OGT expression negatively correlated with CD8+ T cell infiltration.
source: Using TIMER2.0 (http://timer.cistrome.org) analysis, we found that OGT expression negatively correlated with CD8+ T cell infiltration (Figure 6U).
evidence: This claim is supported by TIMER2.0 analysis data shown in Figure 6U.

claim: T cell activation, response to interferon-gamma, interferon-gamma production, antigen processing and presentation, and interleukin-1/12 production are negatively correlated with OGT expression.
source: Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) showed that T cell activation, response to interferon-gamma, interferon-gamma production, antigen processing and presentation, interleukin-1/12 production, dectin-1-mediated noncanonical NF-κB signaling are negatively correlated with OGT expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B-H), while mismatch repair, covalent chromatin modification and DNA repair complex are positively correlated with OGT expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 4I-K).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4B-H.

claim: CD8A, IFNG, ISG15, MX1, CD274, and CXCL10 expression are negatively correlated with OGT expression.
source: Of our most interest, we found that CD8A, IFNG, ISG15, MX1, CD274, and CXCL10 expression are negatively correlated with OGT expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 4L-Qf).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAseq analysis data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4L-Q.

claim: Treatment with OSMI-1 significantly induced cytosolic DNA accumulation.
source: We stained cytosolic dsDNA with anti-dsDNA and found that treatment with OSMI-1 could significantly induce a high percentage of cytosolic DNA accumulation (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence staining data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: γH2AX was obviously increased in OSMI-1-treated cells.
source: We next examined the DNA damage and found that γH2AX was obviously increased in OSMI-1-treated cells (Figure 7B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B–C.

claim: OSMI-1 significantly induced immense DNA strand breakage in treated cells as shown by anti-γH2AX immunofluorescence staining.
source: We also performed the anti-γH2AX immunofluorescence staining and found that OSMI-1 significantly induced immense DNA strand breakage in treated cells (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: OSMI-1 treatment activated cGAS/STING pathway as indicated by increased phosphorylation of STAT1, TBK1, and IRF3 and reduced STING expression.
source: To investigate whether OSMI-1 activated cGAS/STING pathway, we examined activation of major regulators of the pathway in OSMI-1-treated MC38 and LLC cells, as indicated by increased phosphorylation of STAT1, TBK1, and IRF3 and reduced STING expression (Figure 7B–C), which is consistent with Ogt knockout cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B–C.

claim: OSMI-1 alone significantly inhibited MC38 tumor growth and survival, and the combination of OSMI-1 and anti-PD-L1 therapy resulted in superior tumor suppression compared with monotherapy.
source: To our surprise, similar to anti-PD-L1 therapy, OSMI-1 alone significantly inhibited MC38 tumor growth and survival, and the combination of OSMI-1 and anti-PD-L1 therapy resulted in superior tumor suppression compared with monotherapy (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo tumor growth and survival data shown in Figure 7E–F.

claim: Proportion of CD4+ T and CD8+ T cells was increased in OSMI-1, anti-PD-L1 treatment alone and combined treatment in MC38 tumors.
